extracted.intended_audience: legal practitioners, journalists, and historians interested in early-20th-century news-agency operational rules and evidentiary practices
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes operational rules, customary practices, and ethical/procedural norms used by wire services (Associated Press, International News Service) and newspaper telegraph operators in early 20th-century newsrooms, as described in court affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP operator duty to transmit news to AP headquarters
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated Press operators are instructed verbally and by printed rules to transmit over the A.P. wires to A.P. headquarters 'any and all news which may come into their possession' and to perform this duty even when the news originated with another service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiant Henry E. Leary: 'Associated Press operators are instructed verbally and by means of printed rules that they are supposed to transmit ... any and all news which may come into their possession,' and he 'never heard that this news was supposed to exclude news furnished by International News Service or any other news agency.' This establishes an operational expectation that local operators forward tips/news to AP HQ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedence procedure for tips (signal '95' and breaking in)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators with news tips are authorized to 'break in' on the middle of any news item and use a special signal (reported as '95') to indicate that the message is entitled to absolute precedence over any other message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leary: such tips were considered so important that an operator wishing to send one 'was authorized by the rules of the Associated Press to break in on the middle of any news item' and would signal '95' to indicate precedence; operators at different points would contend for the circuit to inform AP headquarters of an opposition story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on printing AP-wire items before fixed time
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AP rules (as applied by member papers), a newspaper was prevented from printing before a certain time (example given: 10:00 a.m.) any news item carried on the Associated Press wire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benjamin E. Gushing explained: 'the rules of the Associated Press prevented the News from printing before 10:00 a.m. any news item carried on the Associated Press wire'; this could lead an editor to seek alternative service copy (e.g., INS) for earlier editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tipping-off practice via telephone/pneumatic tube
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors or telegraph editors would communicate (by telephone or pneumatic tube) the substance of stories carried on one wire service (e.g., INS) to Associated Press offices when the item had not yet appeared on AP bulletins (e.g., 'Hearst is carrying such and such... What have you got?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple affidavits (Anson, Shimansky, Gushing) describe B. E. Gushing and others calling the AP office and advising of INS stories, using phone or pneumatic tube; this was a recurring newsroom practice used to alert AP to competing stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of a 'tip' (from news service parlance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'tip' is a despatch containing, briefly, the substance of a story and frequently an indication of its point of origin; in some instances a tip could be extended enough that AP could write and send the story without further independent inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit text: 'A "tip", in news service parlance, means a despatch containing, in a brief manner, the substance of the nature and character of a story and is frequently accompanied by an indication as to its point of origin.' Also: 'In some ... the matter sent out ... was more than a tip ... such an extended report ... that the Associated Press could write the story ... without making any independent inquiry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial verification when services carry conflicting reports
rubrics_metrics.description: When competing wire services carry contradictory reports, editors would notify both services and request verification to avoid printing incorrect facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benjamin E. Gushing related that, in the case of conflicting reports (e.g., Adamson Law decision), he 'notified both the Associated Press and International News Service of the conflict and asked both Services to verify their stories, so as to avoid having the News print a story containing incorrect facts.' This establishes a newsroom verification practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator incentive and credit for sending tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Tips sent by local operators to AP headquarters were credited to the operator's record and counted in their advancement by the Associated Press, creating an incentive to forward items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kent R. Cochran recounts operators (Cox, Muggeridge) stating that 'the stories so tipped, were credited to their record and counted in their advancement by The Associated Press,' which helps explain the motivation behind tipping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality risks from shared telegraph rooms and loud vs. silent sounders
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple news-service wires and instruments were located in the same telegraph room and operators used loud sounders (audible clicks), a neighboring operator could hear incoming messages and thus learn and pass along rival-service copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits (Warnock, Loomis, Victor Loomis) describe loops of INS and AP wires into the same telegraph room and note that loud sounders' clicks could be heard by nearby operators; Victor Loomis explains loud vs silent sounders and that loud sounders could be heard more than ten feet away, creating an avenue for unintended disclosure or deliberate tipping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of re-disseminating tipped material as AP copy without credit to originator
rubrics_metrics.description: When AP received tips derived from another service's copy, AP headquarters would often send out a story 'basically identical' to the original but bearing no indication it originated with the other service, thus denying credit to the originating agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kent R. Cochran: operators who tipped 'would receive in a short time thereafter, from the central office of The Associated Press, a story basically identical with the International News Service story ... These stories ... would bear no indication that they had originated with the International News Service, and no credit would be given.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting supplemental or alternative agency copy when AP copy is insufficient for edition deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors would request fuller or alternative accounts from another news service (e.g., INS) when AP copy was too meager or restricted by timing to serve an edition's deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gushing asked INS for fuller copy about the Quaker Oats plant explosion and requested an INS story about the 'Powhatan' incident so the News could carry it in an earlier edition because AP copy could not be used for the first edition due to timing rules.
